articles.title: Nine relatives inherited a 49-acre family property in North Carolina, but one sought its sale; now a $950,000 deal threatens to displace family members who say the land holds generations of memories
articles.summary: A decades-old family property dispute in North Carolina has resurfaced after a proposed $950,000 sale of nearly 49 acres near Ocean Isle Beach brought
articles.body: A decades-old family property dispute in North Carolina has resurfaced after a proposed $950,000 sale of nearly 49 acres near Ocean Isle Beach brought relatives into conflict over land they say has been part of their family's history for generations. The property, known as the Jackson-Hill Tract, has nine owners, but only one originally sought its sale through a court-ordered partition proceeding. Now, a developer wants to build 130 homes on the site, where at least five family members still live. Several relatives say they were unaware that the sale process had continued after the original petitioner died and have questioned how the transaction was handled. The dispute has prompted county commissioners to delay consideration of the development.How a family property dispute began nearly 20 years agoThe dispute centres on a 49-acre property at 7436 Ocean Highway West in Brunswick County. The land was divided among nine owners, including members of the Hill family and their descendants. In 2006, the property was surveyed and divided into separate ownership interests.The disagreement over selling the land began around 2008, when one of the owners, Evelyn Hill Williams, sought a court-ordered partition and sale. The matter went before Brunswick County Superior Court, where a judge authorised the sale after determining that physically dividing the property was not feasible because of its condition and other constraints.Attorney Tonia Trest Twigg, who represented Williams in the partition proceedings, was appointed to handle the sale. Williams later died, but the court-appointed process continued. Under North Carolina law, a court-appointed representative can continue certain proceedings after the death of a party, subject to the applicable legal requirements.Relatives say they did not know the sale process was continuingSeveral family members told Brunswick County commissioners that they believed the partition proceedings had ended after Williams' death. They said they only learnt that the property was still being marketed when they received notification about the proposed sale.The relatives also questioned whether Twigg, who had originally been appointed through Williams' case, was entitled to represent the interests of all nine owners. The family's position is that she had been engaged to represent Williams and should not automatically be regarded as representing every co-owner.However, the developer's attorney argued that the court had already authorised the sale and appointed the person responsible for carrying it out. He maintained that the transaction could proceed under the existing court order.The disagreement became a central issue at a November 16 Brunswick County commissioners' meeting, where around a dozen family members and the developer's representatives debated the property's ownership and the proposed development.A $950,000 deal could make way for 130 homesThe proposed buyer, Aston Holding LLC, wants to develop the property as the Jackson-Hill Tract, a residential project featuring 130 single-family homes across four parcels.The proposed transaction is valued at $950,000, although the sale was still pending as of the November 25 report. The developer's attorney said the planned development would use fewer homes than the maximum permitted under the applicable development rules. He also said the project would preserve 23.5 acres as open space, including approximately 10 acres of wetlands.The proposal has raised questions beyond the family dispute. County commissioners also discussed concerns about wetlands, road access and whether the development's cul-de-sacs would accommodate emergency and waste-collection vehicles.The developer's attorney argued that seeking development approval before the property transaction was formally completed was normal practice. He also said the court had already settled the question of whether the land should be sold.Family members say the property holds generations of memoriesFor relatives opposing the sale, the dispute is about more than the money that could be received from the transaction. They described the property as a place where several generations of their family had lived, gathered and built memories.Linwood Hill, one of the property owners who still lives on the land, said his family had worked hard for it and that his father would not have approved of its sale. His daughter, Twanda Williams, told commissioners that no family member wanted the property sold.Herman Douglas Bland, another relative, described the land as the last remaining piece of the family's history. He recalled visiting his grandmother there during childhood summers, when she would wait by the door for relatives arriving from Newark, New Jersey. He also remembered eating cucumbers and tomatoes grown in the family's garden.Bland said relatives had been born in the house and that one young family member had died there. He argued that the memories attached to the property could not be replaced by money received from its sale.Residents face possible displacement as county delays development decisionAt least five people continue to live on the property, including Linwood Hill. Family members told commissioners they had received notices on November 14 informing them that they needed to leave by January.The prospect of relocation added urgency to the relatives' objections. Commissioner Marty Cooke questioned the circumstances surrounding the proposed development and said the county needed greater clarity about who had the authority to sell the property.After nearly an hour and a half of discussion, Brunswick County commissioners unanimously voted to postpone consideration of the development proposal until January 19, 2027. The delay is intended to give the parties time to clarify the ownership dispute.The postponement does not cancel the court-authorised sale or automatically restore control of the land to the relatives. Family members said they were seeking legal representation to return to court and challenge or reopen the partition proceedings.For now, the proposed 130-home development remains on hold while the dispute over the family's 49-acre property continues.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1988, hail and heavy rain knocked out both engines of a TACA Boeing at 16,000 feet; its pilots made a powerless landing on a levee near New Orleans
articles.summary: Discover how TACA Flight in 1988 overcame a harrowing double engine failure due to hail and heavy rain, resulting in a miraculous landing on a Mississippi River levee without injuries.
articles.body: Rain streaking across a plane window rarely worries anyone. Passengers just expect the engines to keep running no matter what the sky throws at them. That expectation failed over Louisiana on 24 May 1988. The Federal Aviation Administration's lessons learned page on TACA Flight 110 tells the story of a Boeing 737-300 that lost power in both engines while descending towards New Orleans. The agency said none of the 38 passengers and seven crew members were injured. So how did a jet with no engine power land safely, and what did the scare teach the aviation industry?A routine descent turned dangerousThe flight began in San Salvador, El Salvador, stopped in Belize City and continued towards New Orleans. The flight went normally until the descent from 35,000 feet. The FAA said the crew tried to avoid the worst storm cells but still found itself flying briefly in very heavy precipitation. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) added in its Brief of Incident that, according to the readings of weather radar, some red cells on either side of the route were spotted, and the crew decided to take a path between two of those. The FAA's account placed the power loss at roughly 16,000 feet after the jet ran into around 30 seconds of heavy hail. Both engines lost power, and the flight crew declared an emergency at 12,000 feet and radioed air traffic control (ATC).Failed restarts and a landing on a leveeFirst, the pilots tried to restart both engines using the air rushing past the plane. But that did not work. Then they started the auxiliary power unit, a small onboard power source, and tried again with starter help. The engines lit up but would not speed up to idle because water and hail were still passing through them. According to the FAA, this attempt pushed engine temperatures beyond safe limits and melted turbine parts. The pilots reduced the throttle and then shut down both engines after seeing no response from the throttle. They realised the airport was too far away and started preparing to ditch. They burst through the cloud layer and saw a small levee. The FAA called the result a successful dead-stick landing, meaning the jet landed without power on a levee near New Orleans. The NTSB brief listed the damage to the aircraft as minor.Why did the engines shut down?According to the NTSB, the probable cause of the accident is double-engine flameout due to water ingestion following exposure to heavy rain and hail. The FAA believed that the storm was as powerful as rainfall of 30 inches, or approximately 76 centimetres per hour. However, hail worked better than rain in terms of getting through the engine core. Hail acts more like a bullet and therefore does not curve according to the direction of airflow. It can pass through the fan blades right into the core. When the core holds too much water, the fuel can no longer burn, and the flame goes out. Up until this incident, it was believed in the industry that hail and water would behave similarly within an engine.How the lesson changed jet enginesThe NTSB cited inadequate engine design and the FAA’s certification standards for water ingestion as contributing causes. After some testing, CFM International (CFMI), the engine maker, changed the shape of the spinner, added a cutback splitter and more bleed valve doors, all to keep hail and water out of the core. The FAA made these changes mandatory, ordering new flight manual procedures for the 737. In 1998, the FAA issued a tougher rain and hail standard for engines, 14 CFR § 33.78. The FAA also noted the engine had four times the safety margin needed in certification tests, but the method of testing was later found to be flawed. The lesson here is pretty simple: old assumptions must be tested against new designs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 43,000-ton Soviet aircraft carrier became a Chinese amusement park; after the park closed, the Minsk was towed to a new home
articles.summary: Discover the intriguing transformation of the Soviet aircraft carrier Minsk from a Cold War military ship to a tourist attraction in China, and its uncertain future after closing down as an amusement park.
articles.body: Some ships sail into battle. The Minsk found itself in a theme park. The ship entered service in 1978 during the Cold War, as a Soviet warship. Decades later, it became a tourist attraction in China. In an article in the Naval War College Review, Andrew S. Erickson, Abraham M. Denmark, and Gabriel Collins note China's 1998 purchase of the Minsk from a South Korean company. That one deal started one of the most unusual second lives any warship has ever had.From Cold War warship to scrap dealThe Minsk was the second ship of the Soviet Navy’s Kiev-class ships. It served in the Pacific Fleet and carried Yak-38 vertical takeoff fighters and helicopters. It wasn't a flat-deck aircraft carrier of the kind used by the US Navy. Instead, it was a hybrid of a cruiser and an aircraft carrier. Its estimated full load displacement varied between 41,000 and 43,000 tonnes. In 1995, it was sold for scrap to a South Korean company. However, the ship managed to escape the breakers. According to the South China Morning Post, it was bought by a Chinese firm in 1998 and turned into a tourist attraction.Life at Minsk WorldThe carrier was docked in Shenzhen's Sha Tau Kok. Minsk World, a military theme park, opened in 2000. The South China Morning Post said the park was touted as a first for China. When the ship first arrived, more than 30,000 visitors came in a single day, a park worker, Deng Keli, told the Southern Metropolis. When the Minsk reached China, the Chinese Navy didn't have a carrier of its own in service yet, and the rare sight ended up becoming a tourist attraction, Newsweek reported. The good times didn't last. The park’s original owners went bankrupt in 2006, and the ship was sold at auction. It was purchased in 2013 by the Dalian Yongjia Group. The park then ran into financial trouble and was closed in 2016.Why China bought old carriersNot everyone saw these ships as simple tourist stops. In a written statement to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission on 29 March 2007, Erickson stated that China had already purchased four decommissioned aircraft carriers. He suggested that the Minsk and its sister ship Kiev were probably bought to be taken apart and studied for future designs. He emphasised that this was his personal opinion as a scholar, not the official view. The Minsk remained in one piece and became an attraction for visitors. Kiev also became a tourist site in Tianjin.The long tow to a new home The Minsk left Shenzhen on 2 April 2016 for Zhoushan, in Zhejiang province, for a refit. It then reached Nantong, Jiangsu province, on 5 May 2016. It was meant to serve as a centrepiece for a new theme park there. Chinese media reported the project would cost 10 billion yuan and open in 2017. However, the park didn't open on schedule. Plans for the Nantong theme park were left in doubt after a fire broke out on the ship in August 2024 during renovation work, according to the state-run China National Radio. The story shows how quickly a big plan can change. A warship built for the Cold War became a tourist attraction, then a prize passed between owners, and finally a ship waiting for its new purpose. It also shows how military hardware can have a second life far away from its first job. For now, the Minsk’s new chapter remains unwritten.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2010, a turbine failure damaged a Qantas A380’s wing and systems at 7,000 feet; its crew returned the aircraft to Singapore with all 469 people aboard uninjured
articles.summary: Discover how a Qantas A380's critical engine failure at 7,000 feet led to an emergency landing and the safe return of all passengers. Learn about the investigation and insights on crew resource management.
articles.body: On 4 November 2010, a Qantas Airbus A380 was climbing out of Singapore when one of its four engines failed. The aircraft was climbing through 7,000 feet when the number two engine experienced an uncontained failure, according to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB). Debris struck the wing and other areas of the aircraft, damaging its structure and systems. The crew still brought it back to Singapore. All 469 people on board came out uninjured.A routine climb that turned dangerousQantas Flight 32 was a scheduled service from London to Sydney via Singapore. The A380 was on its final leg when it left Singapore. It took off from Changi Airport in the morning. Four minutes later, there was an engine failure, and the cockpit was flooded with warning messages. The damage went beyond one engine. Debris had hit the wing, damaging several systems the crew relied on, so the pilots were facing a cascade of problems at once. Still, the aircraft managed to return to Changi at about 11:47 am local time, less than two hours after it had left.How a tiny pipe caused a huge problemThe ATSB spent more than two years and six months completing the investigation and presented its final report on 27 June 2013. It traced the problem to a thin-walled oil pump in the Rolls-Royce Trent 900 engine. A manufacturing defect had left the wall too thin. Due to this, the pipe cracked, causing an oil leak and resulting in a fire. Then a turbine disc broke apart. Aviation experts call this an uncontained engine failure, meaning that pieces break away and escape the engine casing instead of just staying inside. The bureau also issued safety recommendations to regulators in Europe and the United States.Five pilots and a lot of alertsFive pilots were on the flight deck, including Captain Richard de Crespigny. Alerts kept coming up, and each one needed a careful look. The crew went through them together and checked what the aircraft could still do before returning to land. The plane stopped about 150 metres short of the end of the runway, and emergency crews attended to it. The ATSB report praised the crew for managing the event as a competent team and following standard procedures.What research says about teamworkResearchers have used this flight as an example. A 2020 paper published in the International Journal of Safety and Security Engineering looked at crew resource management, or CRM. CRM involves teamwork, leadership training and decision-making. According to Sikora, Hari, and Hanusch, these skills were shown by the Qantas crew during the engine failure, and all occupants were able to survive the incident without injuries. The paper also arrived at a broader conclusion. It said the leadership and teamwork taught as part of CRM can help to reduce risk in rare and complex emergencies. The researchers were, however, careful. The paper only looked at three accident reports and called this an overview. So it can be a useful guide, but not the final word. This means good equipment is important, but so is how crews use it under pressure.The plane flew againThe damaged aircraft, VH-OQA, didn't remain out of service permanently. It was Qantas's first A380, named Nancy-Bird Walton after an Australian aviation pioneer. The aircraft was repaired in Singapore and returned to Sydney in April 2012, over a year after the incident. It was put back into passenger service later that month. Flight 32 is still used as a case study in crew teamwork. A thin pipe started the problem, but shared decision-making helped end it safely.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1990, Sue Hendrickson discovered a T. rex in South Dakota; seven years later, its skeleton sold at auction for $8.36 million
articles.summary: Explore the incredible story of Sue Hendrickson's discovery of the T. rex skeleton in South Dakota, its record-breaking auction price of $8.36 million, and the ongoing scientific insights it provides.
articles.body: In August 1990, fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson noticed a few large bones sticking out of an eroded bluff in South Dakota. According to the Field Museum in Chicago, she followed a hunch that more was hidden under the surface. She was correct. Seven years later, the skeleton she discovered sold at auction for $8.36 million. The story is about science, money, and one big question: who owns a dinosaur?A lucky find in South DakotaHendrickson was on a commercial excavation trip north of the town of Faith when she stumbled upon the skeleton. The museum reports it took six people 17 days to excavate the bones. The dinosaur was named Sue after its finder, but it wasn't clear if the animal was male or female. The fossils date back to the Cretaceous era, about 67 million years ago. Growth rings in the bones, similar to those of tree rings, indicate that the dinosaur lived for about 28 years, which is at the upper end of a T. rex's life expectancy. Scientists also observed a teenage growth spurt, with the animal reaching full size at 19.Why Sue is such a big dealSue is the largest T. rex skeleton ever found, measuring over 40 feet (12 metres) long and 13 feet (about 4 metres) tall at the hip. It is also the most complete. About 90% of the skeleton by bone volume survived. That means that scientists have 250 of the roughly 380 bones in a T. rex skeleton, including the wishbone. The Field Museum calls Sue the most celebrated T. rex and one of the most famous fossils in the world. Peter Makovicky, the then museum's curator of palaeontology, said some questions about T. rex can only be answered by Sue. Scientists have learned about movement, intelligence, and even body weight from the bones.The fight over who owned SueFinding Sue was one thing; deciding who owned it was another. Three parties began a five-year struggle for custody after the find that ended in an auction in 1997. A 2020 article published by Elizabeth D. Jones in History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences analyses the legal battles in the 1990s. Jones notes that, according to her research, academic palaeontologists, fossil collectors, Native Americans, private citizens, and government officials all claimed ownership of Sue. She argues that the debates were started and kept going by assumptions of ownership, expertise, or both.A record-breaking auctionThe public auction took place in 1997. The Field Museum won, with support from McDonald’s Corporation, Walt Disney World Resort, and private donors. The final price came to about $8.4 million, or $8.36 million to be exact. That was the most money ever paid for a fossil at an auction at the time. Following the sale, 12 museum preparators spent more than 30,000 hours preparing the skeleton and another 20,000 hours building the exhibit. The dinosaur was unveiled in the museum's Stanley Field Hall on 17 May 2000. The skeleton is now on display in the Evolving Planet gallery.What Sue is still teaching scientistsSue’s work is far from over. In 2016, one of the small forelimbs was scanned at the Argonne National Laboratory in Lemont, Illinois. Micro-CT scans revealed detailed images of the bone’s interior, helping scientists understand how T. rex used its arms. The actual skull, weighing 600 pounds (about 272 kilograms), is kept separately in a case for visiting scientists to study. Some scientists thought that the holes in the lower jaw were bite marks. However, it is now more commonly believed that they were the result of an infection. The museum adds that it cannot wait to find out what discoveries the skeleton will lead to next.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Indonesia  disaster: 13 dead, 13 still trapped after rain floods illegal gold mine
articles.summary: At least 13 people were confirmed dead and 13 still remain trapped underground after an illegal gold mine in Indonesia got flooded.
articles.body: At least 13 people were confirmed dead and 13 still remain trapped underground after an illegal gold mine in Indonesia got flooded.A total of 26 workers had entered the mine in the Pongkor area of Bogor regency, about 60km south of Jakarta, on Monday when heavy rain caused the nearby Ciseureuh River to overflow and inundate the shaft, leaving them trapped at a depth of around 100 metres.West Java police chief Hengki told Reuters that six of the 13 workers who died had been identified. The search would continue on Thursday, weather permitting.Rescue teams have been focusing on two mine shafts and using ropes to reach the underground areas. The depth of the excavation, along with narrow, slippery and poorly lit passages, has complicated efforts to reach those still trapped.The incident occurred at an unauthorised mining site near facilities operated by state-owned miner Antam’s Pongkor gold mining unit. Antam said the mine was not part of its operations.Rescue efforts delayed after floodingThe flooding initially prompted local miners and residents to try pumping water out of the shaft themselves. Authorities were not immediately alerted because the mine was operating illegally, officials said.Police received reports of workers trapped underground about 16 hours after the flooding, according to an earlier account from West Java police. A formal report from Antam was sent to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight on Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.Rescuers deployed submersible pumps to drain the shaft and tried to seal openings through which groundwater continued to seep in. The water level had not receded significantly, and officials said draining the excavation could take considerable time.The three bodies recovered on Wednesday in the initial phase of the operation were found at depths of between 30 and 40 metres. The identities of the victims were not immediately known at the time.Antam said all its employees were safe and its operations continued normally. The company said it had repeatedly closed access to illegal mining sites in the area and used patrols, drones and surveillance cameras to deter unauthorised activity.Illegal mining poses recurring safety risksSmall-scale and illegal mining is widespread in Indonesia, where mineral deposits in remote areas provide livelihoods for many people but are difficult for authorities to regulate.Such operations often lack adequate safety measures, leaving miners vulnerable to flooding, landslides and tunnel collapses. Gold ore processing can also involve toxic mercury and cyanide, while workers frequently have little or no protective equipment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A New Jersey railway bridge that entered service in 1910 had to swing open every time large boats needed to pass; 116 years later, a $2.3 billion replacement lets ships and trains pass without the bridge opening
articles.summary: For more than a century, a railway bridge in New Jersey had an unusual problem: whenever boats needed to travel along the river below, the entire bridge
articles.body: For more than a century, a railway bridge in New Jersey had an unusual problem: whenever boats needed to travel along the river below, the entire bridge had to swing open, interrupting train services. Having entered service in 1910, the ageing structure became a recurring source of delays for commuters travelling between New Jersey and New York. Now, after years of construction, a $2.3 billion replacement has entered full service, allowing trains and marine traffic to move independently.According to an announcement by Amtrak and NJ TRANSIT on November 16, 2026, both tracks of the new Portal North Bridge are now operational. The fixed-span structure replaces the 116-year-old Portal Bridge over the Hackensack River in Kearny, New Jersey. Its elevated design allows boats to pass underneath without requiring trains to stop for a bridge opening, addressing a longstanding problem along one of the busiest passenger railway corridors in the United States.Why the original Portal Bridge had to open for boatsThe original Portal Bridge was built by the Pennsylvania Railroad and entered service in 1910. It formed an important part of the Northeast Corridor, connecting railway routes between Newark, New Jersey, and New York. Unlike a conventional fixed railway bridge, the Portal Bridge was designed as a movable swing-span structure. It could rotate to create an opening for marine traffic travelling along the Hackensack River. Once the vessels had passed, the bridge had to return to its railway position before trains could resume crossing.Although this arrangement allowed both trains and boats to use the waterway, it created operational difficulties as railway traffic increased over the decades. The ageing bridge also developed mechanical problems and could sometimes fail to close properly after opening. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, more than 450 NJ TRANSIT and Amtrak trains carrying approximately 200,000 passengers crossed the bridge each weekday. A delay caused by a bridge opening or mechanical malfunction could therefore affect a large number of commuters and disrupt services across the wider Northeast Corridor.How the $2.3 billion replacement worksThe new Portal North Bridge was designed to eliminate the need for a movable railway span. Instead of swinging open, it remains permanently in position, with enough clearance for marine vessels to pass beneath it. The new two-track structure rises approximately 50 feet above the Hackensack River, doubling the height clearance available under the original bridge. This allows boats to travel along the river without interrupting railway operations.The replacement project extends approximately 2.44 miles along the Northeast Corridor, including the bridge and its approaches. It also involved constructing retaining walls, concrete piers, deep foundations, steel spans and supporting railway infrastructure. The total project cost is approximately $2.36 billion, funded through federal, state and regional contributions, including investments from the US Department of Transportation, New Jersey and Amtrak. A $1.56 billion construction contract was awarded to the Skanska/Traylor Bros joint venture in October 2021.The project is part of the broader Gateway Program, which aims to modernise and expand passenger railway infrastructure between Newark and New York.Both tracks are now in full serviceThe transition from the original bridge to the replacement took place in stages to maintain railway operations during construction. The first track of the new Portal North Bridge entered service on March 15, 2026, while the old swing bridge continued operating for trains using the second track. The final transfer began on October 9 and was completed on November 16, when both tracks became fully operational.The transition involved five weeks of railway service adjustments, including diversions affecting some NJ TRANSIT commuters travelling towards New York. With the second track now operational, regular service has resumed and the temporary diversions have ended. The new bridge is expected to reduce delays, improve reliability and allow trains to operate more efficiently. It also supports higher train speeds, with the new crossing designed for speeds of up to 90 miles per hour, compared with 60 miles per hour on the original bridge.The 1910 Portal Bridge is scheduled to be dismantled in 2027. Its replacement marks the end of a century-long arrangement in which railway services had to make way for passing vessels. For commuters and river traffic alike, the new crossing represents a significant change: trains can continue moving while boats pass underneath, without either having to wait for the bridge to open or close.You use AI every day. articles.title: Taylor Swift wore a long-discontinued aquarium T-shirt in 'The Life of a Showgirl' film promotion, inspiring fans to revive the 32-year-old design and raise more than $2 million for sea otter conservation
articles.summary: Taylor Swift has sparked an unexpected fundraising success for a Northern California aquarium after wearing a vintage sea otter conservation T-shirt in a
articles.body: Taylor Swift has sparked an unexpected fundraising success for a Northern California aquarium after wearing a vintage sea otter conservation T-shirt in a film celebrating her latest album, The Life of a Showgirl. The Monterey Bay Aquarium re-released the decades-old design following inquiries from fans eager to buy the same shirt. What began as a campaign with a $1.3 million target quickly exceeded expectations, raising more than $2 million in just two days. The proceeds will support the aquarium's efforts to help injured and orphaned sea otters.Taylor Swift's vintage sea otter T-shirt sparks fan frenzyAccording to Fortune, Swift wore the vintage Monterey Bay Aquarium T-shirt in a release party film for her album The Life of a Showgirl. The appearance quickly attracted attention from her fans, who wanted to find the same design, which had last been produced more than 32 years ago.According to Liz MacDonald, the aquarium's director of content strategy, the organisation was inundated with calls from people asking about purchasing the shirt. In response, it relaunched the design on Thursday as part of a special fundraising campaign, setting an initial target of $1.3 million in a nod to Swift's favourite number.Taylor Swift-inspired fundraiser raises $2 million in just two daysThe fundraising campaign exceeded expectations almost immediately. The aquarium reached its $1.3 million target in less than eight hours, with sales averaging approximately $100,000 every 15 minutes, MacDonald said.Donors contributing at least $65.13 to the campaign supporting injured and orphaned sea otters were promised a T-shirt by post. The aquarium subsequently began accepting back-orders, and by Friday afternoon, the total raised had surpassed $2 million, according to its website. The money will support the aquarium's sea otter conservation programme.How Taylor Swift's vintage T-shirt connection remains a mysteryWhile Swift's appearance helped spark the fundraising surge, how she acquired the vintage garment remains unclear. The shirt had not been produced for more than 32 years, dating back to a time when the singer was just three years old.Swift and her fiancé, Travis Kelce, have previously been documented visiting nearby Carmel. However, MacDonald said the aquarium was unaware of the couple having visited its shop. Staff members have also been speculating about what prompted Swift to wear the particular design.One theory involves Opal, a sea otter at the aquarium whose name was selected by fans through an online poll. MacDonald wondered whether Swift might have participated in the vote, pointing out that Opal is Kelce's birthstone and that Opalite is also the name of one of Swift's songs.Liberty Graphics ramps up production to meet Taylor Swift T-shirt demandThe aquarium is working with Liberty Graphics, an employee-owned T-shirt printing company based in Maine, to meet the unexpected demand. The company and the aquarium were both taken by surprise by the scale of interest generated by Swift's appearance.MacDonald said the opportunity had created a moment that could benefit both sea otters and wider ocean conservation efforts. The shirts will be made using 100% cotton and water-based ink, which she described as more ocean-friendly and sustainable. The aquarium is also working to ensure that the packaging does not contain plastic.Liberty Graphics normally produces around 1,500 shirts a day, according to company manager Matt Enos. However, the surge in orders means the business expects to devote most of its resources to fulfilling requests from Swift's fans, beginning Monday. Enos acknowledged that the company had not anticipated such an enormous response, saying: "We definitely didn't envision something this big, but it's a pretty good problem to have."You use AI every day. articles.title: A British woman flew to Florida after two years of messaging a man online about her desire to be killed; she was found stabbed in a shallow grave days later, and he has now been sentenced to two consecutive life terms
articles.summary: A British woman who flew to Florida after about two years of communication with a man has been found buried in a shallow grave, and that man has now been
articles.body: A British woman who flew to Florida after about two years of communication with a man has been found buried in a shallow grave, and that man has now been sentenced to two consecutive life terms. According to the State Attorney's Office of Florida's Fifth Judicial Circuit, a jury found 54-year-old Dwain Chadwick Hall guilty of premeditated first-degree murder and kidnapping. The victim, Sonia Exelby, a 32-year-old British national from Portsmouth, was reported missing in October 2025. Her body was found in Marion Oaks on 17 October 2025. Judge Timothy McCourt passed sentence following the verdict.How did Sonia Exelby end up in Gainesville, FloridaThe State Attorney's Office states that the case began on 13 October 2025. On that date, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) Gainesville Field Office received a request for investigative assistance from Interpol about a missing and endangered woman, identified as Sonia Exelby. She had been reported missing from her home in Portsmouth, England.According to the office, Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary started the investigation and found that Ms Exelby had flown to Gainesville, Florida, three days earlier. Officials then obtained her recent credit card transactions. These showed an Airbnb payment for a rental home in Reddick, and FDLE agents went to the address to search the property.How did investigators uncover Hall's two-year connection to Sonia ExelbyWhile the scene was being processed, the State Attorney's Office says authorities followed up on other transactions on Ms Exelby's account. These included several declined transactions from an auto repair business owned and operated by Hall. Investigators began looking into Hall and, according to the office, found substantial ties to Ms Exelby, even though Hall initially denied knowing her.The office says detectives pieced together cell phone and online records. These established that Ms Exelby, who suffered from mental health issues, had been communicating with Hall for approximately two years. After she arrived at Gainesville Regional Airport, Hall picked her up and drove her to the Airbnb. Officials also determined that Hall had bought items, including rope and a shovel, before she arrived.How did investigators link Hall to Sonia Exelby's murderAccording to the State Attorney's Office, the investigation involved FDLE, the Marion County Sheriff's Office and authorities in the United Kingdom. Ms Exelby's body was found buried in a shallow grave in a wooded area of Marion Oaks on 17 October 2025. Crime scene personnel found a label from a shovel in the grave. It was later matched to a receipt for a purchase made by Hall, which had been captured on a surveillance camera. The shovel was recovered from Hall's residence, and examiners found blood matching Ms Exelby's on its handle.The office says an autopsy determined that Ms Exelby suffered four sharp-force injuries and that her death was ruled a homicide. Investigators also discovered that Hall had mailed a knife to a friend out of state. Authorities recovered it, and it was later determined to be the murder weapon. Hall was promptly arrested and charged. Assistant State Attorneys Amy Berndt and Richard Buxman prosecuted the case. The office credited the work of the Marion County Sheriff's Office, especially Detective Joseph Miller, and of the office of FDLE Commissioner Larry Keefe, including lead investigator Rebekah McKinzie.Disclaimer: This article is based on information made publicly available by the State Attorney's Office of Florida's Fifth Judicial Circuit. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the investigation, the evidence presented, the circumstances of the case, or the court proceedings mentioned. The information should not be interpreted as confirmation from the family of Sonia Exelby, Dwain Chadwick Hall or his legal representatives, or any of the investigating agencies involved.You use AI every day. articles.title: A woman bought a ring for £1 at a British charity shop, believing it was costume jewellery; an expert discovered it was a 22-carat gold Mughal ring with diamonds and rubies worth £2,000
articles.summary: A regular charity shop accessory turned out to be a forgotten piece of jewellery, transforming a £1 purchase into an extraordinary discovery.
articles.body: A regular charity shop accessory turned out to be a forgotten piece of jewellery, transforming a £1 purchase into an extraordinary discovery. What its owner initially considered an attractive piece of costume jewellery was later identified as a rare Indian gold ring featuring precious stones, with an estimated value of £2,000. The incredible find was revealed on the BBC’s Antiques Roadshow, which demonstrated how valuable historical objects can sometimes lie hidden for generations.From charity shop find to historic treasureThe woman appeared on the program with a ring she bought for just £1 from a local charity shop, reports The Mirror UK. She said she saw it amongst the costume jewellery and bought it because she liked the look of it.However, jewellery expert John Benjamin spotted odd features suggesting the piece was far older and more valuable than its modest appearance suggested. Later, he turned the ring over to look at the distinctive fluted reverse and saw that it was decorated with a sunburst pattern, a hallmark of jewellery made in the Georgian period, around 1790-1800, the BBC reports.The discovery led to a more detailed study of its structure, materials, and decorative stones, which finally confirmed its association with the historic Indian craft.Expert finds gold, diamonds and rubiesThe Mirror UK said Benjamin identified the ring as an Indian-made piece in 22-carat bright yellow gold.At first its central stone looked dull and gray, surrounded by a number of smaller red ones. However, further investigation with a thermal-testing method established that the central stone was a diamond, while the surrounding stones were identified as rubies, the online report explains.The expert then identified the jewellery as a Mughal ring, linking the design and origin of the piece to the historic Indian empire. The identification made the find all the more significant as it was not just any piece of ancient gold jewelry, but one which could be attributed to a specific historical period of craftsmanship. Benjamin valued it at some £2,000 – an extraordinary return on the woman’s original £1.Bargain hunting pays unexpected dividendsThe Mughal ring seen on Antiques Roadshow shows the unexpected value that can be found in overlooked charity shop collections. The £2,000 valuation of the historic ring reminds us that what might seem like everyday second-hand jewellry can often have extraordinary historical and monetary value.Image Courtesy: Daily ExpressYou use AI every day. articles.title: An Australian fish hatchery that had failed to raise barramundi for more than five years finally released 3,000 young fish into Gulf wetlands after a former commercial fisher reworked the breeding programme
articles.summary: For more than five years, the tanks at the Les Wilson Barramundi Discovery Centre in Karumba, northern Queensland, produced no baby barramundi at all.
articles.body: For more than five years, the tanks at the Les Wilson Barramundi Discovery Centre in Karumba, northern Queensland, produced no baby barramundi at all. Last week, 3,000 of them went into the Gulf wetlands. The man behind the turnaround is David Hammann, a former commercial fisherman who had never trained in aquaculture.A hatchery that kept stallingThe Les Wilson Barramundi Discovery Centre in Karumba is the only Barramundi hatchery in the world that breeds the Southern Gulf type of the barramundi. The centre was started by a group of commercial fishermen using second hand, donated equipment. Their aim was simple: restock local waterways with fingerlings to maintain a sustainable fishing stock for years to come. According to the Centre’s website, they came to be known as the Gulf Barramundi Restocking Association.Carpentaria Shire Council took it over in 2012. The early years went well enough, but staffing gaps and repeated breeding failures wore down production. By 2020 it had stopped producing fingerlings entirely.Mayor Jack Bawden told ABC News that there was always a reason the fish weren't spawning. The council, he said, didn't understand fish biology well enough to find the fix.The Centre is now more than a breeding centre, it has become a major recreational spot for the small gulf town with displays of history, stories, lifecycle and habits of these iconic fishes. Visitors can also see how the fish are caught, raised and released.The fisher who got the jobAfter failing to release a single hatchling for consequent years, the council promoted Hammann last year. He did not have any institutional aquaculture qualifications, but he knew the behaviour and biology of the fish because of his years of experience with it. According to ABC News, he spent the following year experimenting with tank sizes, new broodstock and techniques he described as “local secrets.”According to ABC News, his team collected wild barramundi from the Southern Gulf of Carpentaria and sorted the males from the females. They checked the females' eggs and kept the ones with eggs of around 400 microns or larger. Those selected fish received hormone injections to prompt spawning. This time the spawning worked, and the hatchery raised fingerlings ready for release.Why these young barramundi matterThe Mayor admitted that 3,000 doesn't sound like much. After five years of nothing, though, he called it a significant “improvement.”The mission is also crucial because the centre specifically breeds Southern Gulf of Carpentaria barramundi, which is a regional breed. It is distinct from the fish on Australia’s east coast, which needs warmer water.Another precaution taken by Hammann was to choose wetlands for the release of these fingerlings. The reeds and natural structures in the wetlands give the fingerlings cover from predators.Others in the region are waitingBefore production stopped in 2020, the centre sold affordable fingerlings to fishing groups in Mount Isa and Cloncurry, who stocked local lakes and dams with them. Lake Moondarra, near Mount Isa, hasn't received new barramundi for several years. Big fish are still there, but anglers have noticed a shortage of small and medium ones.Mick Scotney, president of the Mount Isa Fish Stocking Committee, told ABC News that bringing fingerling production back would improve the fishing. It would also give the water a healthier mix of sizes. He pointed out that large fish are more vulnerable to fish kills in cold winters and low water, so a lake that depends on ageing fish carries real risk.What comes nextThe centre has permits to release up to 100,000 barramundi into the Norman River and another 100,000 around Burketown. He wants to work towards those numbers in the next breeding season, and Mount Isa and Cloncurry fishing groups would stand to benefit if he gets there.The first 3,000 fish won't cover the region's stocking needs, but they show the hatchery can breed fish again. For Karumba, a town built around fishing, that is where recovery starts.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Pro-Palestinian protesters clash with Israelis, NYPD at Brooklyn real estate event; several arrested
articles.summary: Several people were arrested after pro-Palestinian protesters clashed with Israeli supporters and New York City police during a demonstration outside a
articles.body: Several people were arrested after pro-Palestinian protesters clashed with Israeli supporters and New York City police during a demonstration outside a kosher deli in Brooklyn on Wednesday night.The confrontation took place outside Essen NY Deli in the Midwood neighbourhood, where Israeli brokerage firm CapitIL was hosting a real estate event. Footage circulating on social media showed groups of protesters and Israeli supporters involved in physical altercations, while demonstrators also clashed with police and tried to push through barricades.The protest was organised by the Palestine Right to Return Coalition of New York and New Jersey, also known as Pal-Awda. The group alleged that the Israeli company was hosting a land sale event featuring properties in settlements in the occupied West Bank.However, a representative of CapitIL told Jewish News Syndicate that the company was not promoting any properties in the region during its visit.Several arrested as protesters clash with policeTensions escalated as demonstrators confronted officers and attempted to breach police barricades. Videos from the scene showed police struggling to contain the crowds, with several protesters being taken away in handcuffs.The New York Police Department (NYPD) confirmed that multiple arrests were made during the demonstration but did not immediately disclose the exact number of people detained or the charges they could face.More than 200 police officers were deployed to the area, Israeli media outlet Ynet reported.The NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a specialised unit that has historically handled large demonstrations and violent crowd confrontations, was also deployed during the protest.New York City Councilwoman Inna Vernikov condemned the demonstration, alleging that it turned violent and featured anti-Jewish slogans, including "Intifada" and "F the Jews". In a post on X, she said four arrests had been made and that the SRG had been called to the scene.In a subsequent post, Vernikov criticised Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to disband the unit, arguing that Wednesday's confrontation demonstrated why it was needed to protect Jewish-owned businesses.Mamdani's plan to replace specialised police unitThe deployment comes amid controversy surrounding Mamdani's campaign promise to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group.Although the mayor announced plans to dismantle the unit, the transition is not expected to be completed until spring 2027, ABC7 reported.City Hall has said the SRG will be replaced by a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division and a specialised 30-member police team called the First Amendment Support Team. The latter will operate under the NYPD's Community Affairs Bureau.A separate Patrol Support Division will also be established within the NYPD's Patrol Services Bureau, with officers receiving specialised crowd-management training.The clashes also come against the backdrop of rising concerns over antisemitism in New York. According to figures cited in the report, the Anti-Defamation League recorded 860 antisemitic incidents across New York City in 2025, including 278 in Brooklyn.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war: 10 reasons why peace remains elusive and how the conflict could end
articles.summary: Nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the war remains far from over.
articles.body: Nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the war remains far from over. Territorial disputes, Nato membership, security guarantees and competing geopolitical interests continue to prevent a peace agreement. While US President Donald Trump has renewed efforts to bring Moscow and Kyiv to the negotiating table, neither side appears ready to make the concessions required to end the conflict.The war, which began on February 24, 2022, has evolved into a prolonged confrontation involving Russia's territorial ambitions, Ukraine's fight to preserve its sovereignty and a wider contest between Moscow and the West.The latest diplomatic efforts have failed to resolve the fundamental disagreements. Russia wants Ukraine to abandon its Nato ambitions and make territorial concessions, while Kyiv insists that any settlement must protect its sovereignty and provide credible security guarantees. European countries, meanwhile, fear that an agreement favouring Moscow could create further security threats across the continent.In a conversation with The Times of India, Professor Rajan Kumar explained why the war continues, Europe's role in the conflict, Russia's demands and what a possible settlement could look like.Here are 10 key reasons behind the continuing conflict1. Russia and Ukraine have fundamentally different ideas about the country's futureAt the heart of the conflict is a disagreement over Ukraine's political identity and its place in the international order.Russia has historically considered Ukraine an important part of its strategic neighbourhood. The two countries share centuries of intertwined political, cultural and economic history, including their common past within the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union.Ukraine, which became independent following the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, has increasingly sought closer political, economic and military integration with Europe.The disagreement became particularly visible in 2013-14, when then Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych abandoned plans to sign an association agreement with the European Union following pressure from Moscow. The decision triggered mass protests, known as the Euromaidan movement, and Yanukovych was removed from power in February 2014.Russia subsequently annexed Crimea and supported separatist forces in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk regions. The developments marked the beginning of a conflict that eventually escalated into Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.2. Nato membership remains the biggest sticking pointOne of the central reasons behind Russia's opposition to Ukraine's Western integration is its potential membership of Nato.At the 2008 Bucharest summit, Nato declared that Ukraine and Georgia would eventually become members of the alliance, although neither received an immediate membership invitation.Russia has consistently opposed Ukraine joining the military alliance, arguing that Nato's eastward expansion threatens its security.Professor Rajan Kumar believes Nato membership was the central issue behind Russia's decision to invade Ukraine. However, he argues that Moscow's historical and cultural perception of Ukraine makes the issue particularly sensitive."The main reason why Russia initiated this war was that Ukraine was willing to become a member of Nato, and there was a sense that Nato might give it membership and the European Union might also offer some kind of affiliation to Ukraine."But the main issue is that Russia ethnically considers Ukraine and Belarus to be one people, the Slavic people. It fears that this is an attempt by Europe to create a rift among the Slavic population."Kumar also questioned the argument that Nato's military presence near Russian borders alone explains Moscow's opposition."But just look at the Baltic states. Nato forces are already there, and these countries share borders with Russia. Nato forces are also in Finland, which has a 1,300-km border with Russia."So, when people make this argument, I think they don't think much before making it. But yes, what you said in your first statement is correct. Nato membership for Ukraine was the real issue, not simply that forces would come to the Russian border."3. Crimea and Donbas remain major territorial obstaclesTerritory is arguably the biggest obstacle to a peace agreement.Russia currently controls approximately one-fifth of Ukraine's internationally recognised territory, including Crimea and substantial parts of eastern and southern Ukraine.In September 2022, Moscow announced the annexation of four Ukrainian regions: Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Ukraine and most of the international community rejected the annexations as illegal. Russian forces do not control all the territory within the claimed administrative boundaries.Moscow has demanded that Ukraine withdraw from the remaining parts of Donbas under Kyiv's control. Ukraine, however, has rejected the demand and refuses to legally recognise Russia's territorial claims.The issue has remained central to the latest US-led negotiations.The Financial Times reported on November 25 that the Trump administration had moved away from proposals involving American business investments in Russia as an incentive for peace. The Kremlin had shown little interest in such economic arrangements and continued to insist on territorial concessions from Ukraine.The report said Putin was prepared to end the offensive if Ukraine surrendered the entirety of Donbas, a condition Zelenskyy has repeatedly rejected.4. Europe wants to remain involved and fears a Russian advantageEurope's role has become another important dimension of the conflict.European countries have provided Ukraine with military equipment, financial assistance and diplomatic support. They fear that a settlement allowing Russia to retain its territorial gains could embolden Moscow and create further security threats for the continent.Kumar argues that European countries are reluctant to accept an immediate ceasefire because they believe Russia could emerge stronger from the conflict."The obstacle to this mediation, or any possibility of a ceasefire, is Europe. Europe doesn't want to stop the war immediately. Europe doesn't want the US and Russia to negotiate. Europe is not playing any role [in the negotiations]."Europe also wants Ukraine to remain engaged because most European countries believe that if the Ukraine war ends with some advantage to Russia, which is very likely, the next target would be Europe. So, essentially, Ukraine is fighting the war for Europe at this point in time."He believes European countries are continuing to provide Ukraine with financial and military assistance to sustain its resistance, while avoiding a direct military confrontation with Russia."European countries still somehow believe, wrongly, that there is a possibility of keeping Russia engaged in a situation of deadlock and that, in the long term, this will weaken Putin and Russia. Because of that, they keep supplying basic survival material and weapons to Ukraine."Kumar also argues that Europe wants a place at the negotiating table because it fears that a security arrangement reached directly between Washington and Moscow could leave European countries out of decisions affecting their own security.5. Neither side trusts the other to honour a ceasefireEven if Russia and Ukraine agree to stop fighting, ensuring that the ceasefire lasts will remain a major challenge.Ukraine fears that a temporary pause could allow Russia to regroup, replenish military supplies and prepare for another offensive. Its concerns are partly rooted in the failure of the Minsk agreements, signed in 2014 and 2015 to end fighting in eastern Ukraine.Russia, meanwhile, has accused Ukraine and its Western supporters of using ceasefires to strengthen Kyiv's military position.The two sides also disagree over how a ceasefire would be monitored and enforced. Ukraine wants international monitoring and credible guarantees against renewed Russian aggression, while Moscow has rejected the presence of European or Nato forces on Ukrainian territory.Putin has also questioned the prospect of European peacekeeping forces, arguing that their deployment would undermine the possibility of peace.Without an agreed monitoring mechanism, enforcement arrangements and consequences for violations, a ceasefire could merely freeze the conflict rather than resolve it.6. Ukraine wants security guarantees, but Russia opposes Nato involvementSecurity guarantees have emerged as another major obstacle to negotiations.Ukraine argues that it cannot accept a settlement without assurances that Russia will not launch another invasion. Its preferred option has been Nato membership, which would provide collective defence protection under Article 5.However, Moscow has rejected Ukraine's membership of Nato and opposed the deployment of foreign military forces in the country.Alternative arrangements could involve military assistance, intelligence-sharing, air defence support and commitments from Western countries to respond if Russia attacks again. Ukraine has also sought international security arrangements that could include a role for European forces.Kumar believes this disagreement leaves Ukraine with limited options."If Nato membership is not given, Ukraine is left with very limited options. What Trump and Russia are saying is that Ukraine may be considered for some kind of Nato-like security arrangement, but it will not be given Nato membership."Now, Russia will not agree to that kind of security arrangement if European or Nato forces come to Ukraine for its defence. These are the difficult issues and the thorny issues between the two sides, and that is the reason why negotiations are not progressing."The challenge for negotiators is to find an arrangement that reassures Kyiv without crossing Moscow's stated red lines.7. The battlefield has turned into a war of attritionNeither Russia nor Ukraine has achieved a decisive military victory, turning the conflict into a prolonged war of attrition.Russia failed to capture Kyiv in the opening phase of its February 2022 invasion but subsequently concentrated its military operations in eastern and southern Ukraine.Ukraine recovered territory in parts of the Kharkiv region and Kherson during counteroffensives in 2022. However, it has struggled to achieve another decisive breakthrough.Russia continues to have advantages in manpower, artillery production and ammunition supplies. Ukraine, meanwhile, has increasingly relied on drones, precision strikes and attacks on Russian military logistics and energy infrastructure.According to the November 2026 assessment cited by Al Jazeera, Russian forces captured approximately 117.38 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory during January-October 2026, indicating the difficulty of achieving substantial territorial advances despite continued fighting.The human cost has also mounted. A November 25 NBC News report, citing leaked Russian statistical records analysed by independent media, said at least 490,000 Russian military deaths had been registered in the data. Meduza projected the figure could reach 720,000 when deaths not yet registered were included. NBC said it could not independently authenticate the leaked data or confirm the estimates.Russia has rejected the higher estimates. The actual military death tolls on both sides remain uncertain.8. The human cost is mounting, but domestic pressure has not forced a settlementThe war has killed and injured thousands of civilians and displaced millions of Ukrainians.According to figures compiled by Russia Matters in its November 24 war report, more than 17,000 civilians had been killed and nearly 54,000 injured in Ukraine. Approximately 9.6 million Ukrainians remain displaced, including 3.7 million internally displaced people and 5.9 million refugees abroad.Military casualties are considerably harder to establish because neither country regularly publishes comprehensive figures.Kumar believes growing public fatigue could eventually put pressure on Zelenskyy to negotiate, particularly as Ukrainians continue to bear the burden of mobilisation and fighting."Yes, some people are already tired of the war. Many people, if there is a normal situation, don't want to die. Most people don't want to die for the sake of anything. If they have lost their families, what is the meaning of continuing?"But when there is a war-like situation, the press is not free. You cannot speak against the army or the regime because you are treated as a traitor, and under martial law, you can be sent to jail."He added that the pressure on Ukraine's leadership was increasing as the conflict continued."People are extremely tired. Most people don't want to fight, but because of conscription, state policies and the regime, they are forced to fight a war."9. Energy attacks, sanctions and international partnerships are sustaining the confrontationThe conflict has expanded beyond the battlefield to include energy infrastructure, oil refineries, power plants and supply chains.Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian electricity and gas infrastructure, particularly ahead of winter. Ukraine has responded with drone strikes targeting Russian refineries, military logistics and energy facilities. The attacks are aimed at weakening the other side's ability to sustain the war.Western sanctions have also increased pressure on the Russian economy. However, Moscow has maintained trade and diplomatic relationships with countries outside the Western sanctions framework, including China and India.Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to depend on European financial and military assistance as uncertainty surrounds the scale of future American support.Trump's approach has also changed the diplomatic environment. His administration has prioritised negotiations, while Ukraine remains concerned that reduced US assistance could weaken its position.10. Trump's peace efforts face the biggest question: What will Russia and Ukraine gain?The Trump administration has attempted to bring Moscow and Kyiv closer through negotiations, including discussions involving US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.However, the latest diplomatic efforts have failed to resolve the territorial dispute and disagreements over Ukraine's future security arrangements.The Financial Times reported on November 25 that Washington had shelved proposals to use American business investments in Russian oil, titanium and aviation ventures as incentives for peace. The focus has shifted towards more traditional negotiations centred on territory and security.Putin has continued to insist on territorial concessions, while Zelenskyy has rejected demands that would require Ukraine to surrender Donbas.Kumar believes a settlement will eventually emerge through negotiations, but argues that Ukraine may have to accept the loss of territory."Ultimately, all wars end through some kind of negotiation and peace. So, peace will happen. There is no doubt that there will be some kind of ceasefire or agreement."But given the conditions, Russia will not withdraw from Donbas. So, Ukraine will have to accept the loss of territory."Legally, it will be difficult for any regime in Ukraine to accept a truncated territory. But sometimes, when you are dealing with a large neighbour, a big neighbour, you don't have any choice. You establish peace under pressure also. Unfortunately, Ukraine will have to accept that."He also believes Ukraine would need something to present as a political gain to its people if it agrees to territorial concessions."Russia is willing to negotiate. Let me tell you, although if you read most of the Western newspapers, especially European or American publications like The Washington Post and The New York Times, they give the impression that Putin is not willing to negotiate, which is not true."Russia has already made the gains it wanted. Keeping in mind that Russia has now realised that controlling Kyiv will not be easy, it has accepted the new reality and would be happy with a Donbas treaty. It can show its people that at least it gained something."Now, the Ukrainian regime also needs to gain something. So, how does it show that? The only two possibilities are that either Ukraine becomes a member of Nato or gets something similar to that, or Ukraine becomes a member of at least the European Union, so that it can tell its people that it gained something despite making sacrifices."How will the Russia-Ukraine war end?A negotiated settlement remains the most likely way to end the war, but the terms remain deeply contested. Russia wants territorial concessions and an end to Ukraine's Nato ambitions, while Kyiv seeks security guarantees that can prevent another invasion.Professor Rajan Kumar believes Ukraine may eventually have to accept territorial losses, particularly in Donbas, in exchange for a security arrangement or European Union membership. However, such a compromise would be politically difficult for Zelenskyy to sell domestically.If neither side is willing to make these concessions, the conflict could continue as a prolonged war of attrition, with periodic diplomatic efforts failing to produce a lasting settlement.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Jeopardises safety in train operations': North Central Railway warns staff against making reels
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The North Central Railway (NCR) has warned its employees against making and posting social media reels during duty hours, saying the activity
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The North Central Railway (NCR) has warned its employees against making and posting social media reels during duty hours, saying the activity distracts staff and jeopardises train operations.In an advisory issued on November 17, 2027, the railway zone cautioned that employees could face disciplinary action for violating safety protocols or engaging in unauthorised commercial activities through content creation.The communication was addressed to senior officials of its three divisions, Prayagraj, Jhansi and Agra, and its workshops. The zone said some railway employees were creating and posting reels on their social media accounts while on duty, which could compromise operational safety."Performing such activities during duty hours poses a severe distraction, jeopardises safety in train operations, and compromises administrative integrity," the NCR zone said as quoted by PTI.Reels could amount to unauthorised businessThe railway zone also flagged the possibility of employees earning money through social media content, saying this could amount to running an unauthorised commercial enterprise or side business."Moreover, there is a strong likelihood that some staff are deriving monetary advantage through their (social media) content creation, which amounts to running an unauthorised commercial enterprise/side business, which is a direct violation of Rule 15 of the Railway Services (Conduct) Rules, 1966," it said.The zone warned that filming on railway premises or equipment for commercial purposes without formal permission or payment of prescribed fees was prohibited."Filming on Railway premises or equipment for commercial gain without formal permission or without payment of prescribed film shooting/commercial fees is prohibited."It added that if social media posts were found to be generating commercial benefits, the prescribed fees would have to be paid. Failure to do so could invite penal action.Prior approval required for railway-related contentThe NCR zone also clarified that employees creating educational or awareness-related content about the Railways would need prior approval from the competent authority."Posts intended for educational or socio-awareness generation regarding Railways may only be published with the prior approval of the Competent Authority," it said.It further directed employees who frequently post content on social media to submit a formal undertaking to the railway administration."Staff who frequently post content on social media must submit a formal undertaking to the Railway Administration confirming that they derive no monetary advantage from such posts and that their activities do not compromise Railway safety or security."Divisional and workshop authorities have been directed to closely monitor the active social media accounts of railway personnel. The zone warned that employees found violating safety protocols or engaging in social media activities during duty hours would face strict disciplinary action.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: The Kremlin has accused European countries of encouraging Ukraine to continue fighting Russia, claiming that Kyiv has become less inclined to pursue peace negotiations.Moscow said the encouragement had made Ukraine more willing to prolong the war rather than work towards a diplomatic settlement.Earlier Kremlin has also criticised European pledges to maintain military support for Ukraine and impose further sanctions on Russia, arguing that such moves undermine the peace process, Reuters reported.On the possibility of a major prisoner-of-war (POW) exchange, the Kremlin said Russian and Ukrainian intelligence agencies, along with human rights ombudsmen from both countries, were jointly preparing lists of prisoners. The process would be completed soon, it added.Moscow also described alleged Ukrainian attacks in Libya and the Baltic Sea as "very dangerous", saying it had noted attempts by Kyiv to widen the conflict to the Mediterranean and Baltic regions."No one wants this conflict to expand," the Kremlin said.On Russian President Vladimir Putin's possible participation in the G20 summit in the US in December, the Kremlin said no decision had been taken yet.The latest US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine took place in Abu Dhabi on November 11, marking the first direct negotiations between the two sides in nine months. The discussions resulted in an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange, but failed to produce a breakthrough on key issues, including territorial disputes.European participation has emerged as a major point of disagreement. Moscow has questioned what European countries would contribute to the negotiations, while Kyiv has maintained that European involvement is essential to any lasting peace settlement.You use AI every day. articles.title: China's new 8-tonne cargo drone: Why it could change the way wars are fought
articles.summary: Unmanned aircraft now play an essential role in modern warfare, carrying out missions ranging from reconnaissance and surveillance to target
articles.body: Unmanned aircraft now play an essential role in modern warfare, carrying out missions ranging from reconnaissance and surveillance to target identification and strikes.But their role on the battlefield is expanding beyond combat operations. Militaries are exploring their use in logistics, from transporting ammunition and medical supplies to delivering food and equipment to troops in remote and contested areas.China's unveiling of an eight-tonne cargo drone marks another step in this shift, as countries look to integrate unmanned aircraft into military supply operations.The W8000, developed by Chinese aviation company Air White Whale, was unveiled in Zhuhai ahead of the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, scheduled to open on December 7, defence publication The War Zone reported.The twin-turboprop aircraft is designed to carry up to eight metric tonnes of cargo and features a rear loading ramp for transporting bulky equipment and palletised freight.However, the W8000 remains a developmental concept, and its proposed payload capacity has not yet been demonstrated in flight. Its range and maximum takeoff weight have also not been disclosed, TWZ reported.The W8000 follows the company's smaller W5000 cargo drone, which completed its maiden flight on November 14 in Inner Mongolia. The W5000 is designed to carry up to five tonnes of cargo, has a reported maximum range of 2,600 km and a maximum takeoff weight of 10.8 tonnes.Chinese sources have reported that Air White Whale has received 835 orders or prospective commitments for the W5000, with commercial operations targeted for the end of 2027, subject to testing and certification.Why is China developing larger cargo drones?China's push to develop heavy-lift cargo drones is linked to the challenge of supplying troops and maintaining military operations across remote and contested areas.The aircraft could provide the People's Liberation Army (PLA) with another means of transporting ammunition, medical supplies, food, spare parts and equipment to military installations, particularly in remote locations and island outposts in the South China Sea.Their potential value becomes more significant during a conflict, when military bases, ports and conventional supply routes could come under attack. Uncrewed cargo aircraft could help maintain supply operations without exposing pilots to the risks associated with flying into contested areas.They could also support China's military presence across the Indo-Pacific by providing supplies to locations where maintaining regular transport links is difficult.However, their ability to operate in a conflict would depend on their range, payload, survivability and resistance to electronic warfare, including GPS jamming and disruption of communications.China is not alone in the raceThe United States is also developing autonomous cargo aircraft, with military planners looking at their potential to transport supplies to troops operating across remote islands and forward bases in the Indo-Pacific.The US military's interest is driven by the need to maintain supply lines during a conflict, when conventional transport aircraft, ships and logistics infrastructure could face attacks.US aviation company Textron Aviation and autonomy specialist Merlin are developing the Cessna SkyCourier UX, an uncrewed version of the twin-engine SkyCourier. The aircraft is designed to carry around 6,000 pounds (2.7 tonnes) of cargo.The US air force has also explored autonomous Cessna Caravan aircraft for logistics operations in the Pacific, including demonstrations involving Joby Aviation's former Xwing autonomy team.China, meanwhile, is pursuing several cargo drone programmes, including the W5000, W8000, HH-100 and CH-YH1000. The W8000's proposed eight-tonne payload would exceed the stated capacities of the US aircraft discussed above, although it remains a developmental concept.Why cargo drones matter in modern warfareMilitary operations depend on the ability to move ammunition, food, fuel, medical supplies and equipment to troops. In a conflict, these supply lines can become targets, particularly when forces operate across remote islands, forward bases and areas exposed to enemy attacks.Cargo drones could provide another means of maintaining these supply lines. Unlike conventional transport aircraft, uncrewed aircraft do not put pilots at risk during cargo missions. They could also operate alongside crewed aircraft and ships to deliver supplies to locations where conventional transportation is restricted.The US military has identified this challenge as contested logistics. US air force Lieutenant General Kenyon K Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering and force protection, said that "the era of uncontested logistics is over".Bell said the US military would need to sustain its forces while operating under threat, highlighting the need to rethink how supplies are transported during a conflict.US air force chief of staff General Kenneth Wilsbach has also acknowledged the potential of autonomous cargo aircraft in the Pacific, saying the service was evaluating different aircraft demonstrators, although it did not have a programme of record for their procurement at the time.The development of heavy-lift cargo drones could therefore add another component to military airlift capabilities. However, their operational value would depend on payload, range, reliability and their ability to function when communications and satellite navigation systems are disrupted.
